title: James Gosling, the Green Project, and the Oak Tree (early-to-mid 1990s)
explainer: Java began life as 'Oak,' a language James Gosling and Sun's small 'Green Team' built in the early 1990s for embedded, consumer-electronics devices - not for enterprise servers. When a trademark conflict forced a rename and the project was redirected toward the emerging web (where a 'write once, run anywhere' bytecode language was suddenly valuable), the same design choices made for tiny set-top boxes - a small, portable, strongly-typed VM-based language - became the foundation of large-scale enterprise OOP. It's a useful reminder that Java's conservative, explicit style was originally an embedded-systems safety feature, not an enterprise one.

title: Anders Hejlsberg and the Road from Turbo Pascal to C# (1980s-2000)
explainer: C#'s chief designer, Anders Hejlsberg, had already built Turbo Pascal and then led Delphi at Borland before joining Microsoft, where he first worked on Visual J++, Microsoft's own extended implementation of Java. A 1997 lawsuit from Sun over those Java extensions ended the J++ project, and Microsoft's response was to build its own language and platform from scratch - C# and .NET - drawing on Hejlsberg's Object Pascal and Delphi experience rather than Java's. That lineage explains why C# often reads as 'what Java could add once untethered from Sun's spec,' from properties to later language features Java added much later.
